sections.title: Walk the flowchart
sections.intro: A teammate pings you: "my new `checkout` pod has been stuck for five minutes." Work it the way you would live — one observation, one decision at a time.

questions.prompt: You run `kubectl get pods`. Before anything else, which column narrows the problem the most, and why?
questions.snippet:
NAME       READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
checkout   0/1     Pending   0          5m
options: AGE — five minutes means the scheduler gave up
STATUS — Pending means the cluster is out of capacity
READY — 0/1 means the readiness probe is failing
RESTARTS — 0 means no container has ever started
questions.explanation: A restart can only happen after a container started and exited. Zero restarts means the problem is before or during container start, not after. READY 0/1 is true of every pod that hasn't started, so it tells you nothing yet, and Pending has many causes besides capacity.

questions.prompt: Nothing has run yet. What single question splits the rest of the search in half?
options: Has the pod been assigned a node (`spec.nodeName`)?
Is kube-proxy healthy on the node it's on?
Is the namespace over its ResourceQuota?
Does the image tag actually exist in the registry?
questions.explanation: The scheduler's job ends the moment it writes a node name into the pod. No node means a scheduler-side problem; a node means kubelet on that node is stuck. Checking the image first is a guess, since you'd only care about images once a node is trying to pull one.

questions.prompt: `kubectl describe pod checkout` shows `Node: <none>`. Whose logic do you now reason about, and where does it explain itself?
options: kubelet — `journalctl -u kubelet` on the node
The scheduler — its FailedScheduling event on the pod
The runtime — `crictl ps` on the node
kube-proxy — the pod has no network yet
questions.explanation: With no node assigned, kubelet and the runtime have never seen this pod, so there's nothing on any node to read. The scheduler is the only component that has tried, and it reports why in the pod's Events.

questions.prompt: The Events section shows this. What does the wording tell you, and what's your first check?
questions.snippet: Warning  FailedScheduling  60s  default-scheduler  0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient memory.
options: Compare the pod's memory request to what nodes have left
Check `kubectl get nodes` — a node is NotReady
Compare taints and tolerations — memory is a taint
Raise `limits.memory` — the pod hit its limit
questions.explanation: The scheduler compares *requests* against a node's allocatable capacity minus what's already requested. It never looks at limits, and it never looks at live usage. `kubectl describe node` (the Allocated resources section) shows that math. Raising the limit changes nothing about where the pod can be placed.

questions.prompt: The checkout pod requests `memory: 8Gi`. Your teammate admits they copied that from another service and the app actually uses about 600Mi. What do you recommend, and what's the risk?
options: Add a node — it's always the safe choice
Remove the request entirely so it fits anywhere
Lower the request to near real usage; risk is eviction
Add a toleration so it can use reserved nodes
questions.explanation: Lowering a padded request is the cheap fix, but only if the padding is real. That's why you confirm usage first. Removing the request makes the pod BestEffort, the first thing evicted. A toleration doesn't help, because the event never mentioned taints.

questions.prompt: A week later the same symptom shows up, with the same message repeating. The cluster has an autoscaler that should add nodes. What's different now?
questions.snippet:
Warning  FailedScheduling  6m (x14 over 6m)  default-scheduler  0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient cpu.
Normal   NotTriggerScaleUp 6m  cluster-autoscaler  pod didn't trigger scale-up: 1 max node group size reached
options: The autoscaler refused — the node group is at max size
etcd is too slow to register the new nodes
The scheduler is stuck — restart kube-scheduler
The pod's requests are padded again — lower them
questions.explanation: The repetition is the signal: the same correct complaint, no new node. The autoscaler is a separate component and wrote its own event explaining why. Raising the max size is the fix, and the tradeoff is a higher cost ceiling.

questions.prompt: Different pod, different day: `Node: node-2` is set, and STATUS reads `CreateContainerConfigError`. Which part of the system do you now suspect, and what's the likely cause?
options: kubelet — a referenced ConfigMap or Secret is missing
The app — it's crashing during startup
The registry — the image pull is failing
The scheduler — it picked a node that can't run it
questions.explanation: Once a node is set, the scheduler is done. CreateContainerConfigError happens before the runtime is even invoked: kubelet resolves env/volume references first, and one is missing. The app hasn't run, which is why RESTARTS is still 0.

questions.prompt: Last sanity check before you commit to a diagnosis: a pod that was Running fine an hour ago, with no spec change, now has a fresh copy sitting in Pending. What should you look at first?
options: Node health — the old node went NotReady
The image tag — it was retagged upstream
The init containers — one is now hanging
The pod's tolerations — they were changed
questions.explanation: If nothing about the pod changed, the pod probably isn't the problem. A NotReady node causes eviction after about 5 minutes, and the replacement looks exactly like an ordinary scheduling failure. `kubectl get nodes` takes two seconds and saves you from debugging the wrong thing.

sections.title: Read the signal
sections.intro: Each one stands alone. Name what the output points at, and why.

questions.snippet: 0/3 nodes are available: 3 node(s) had untolerated taint {dedicated: gpu-only}.
options: The nodes have run out of GPUs to allocate
The GPU device plugin isn't installed
Pods without a toleration for that taint are kept off
The nodes are missing a `dedicated=gpu-only` label
questions.explanation: Taints are an intentional repel mechanism. The real question is whether this pod belongs on a GPU node at all. Adding a toleration to a general workload just lets it steal the capacity the taint was protecting.

questions.prompt: The pod uses a PVC, and the cluster spans three zones. Why can't the scheduler place it?
questions.snippet: 0/3 nodes are available: 3 node(s) had volume node affinity conflict.
options: The volume's backing disk is full
The PV is pinned to a zone with no node that fits the pod
The PVC was never created in this namespace
`WaitForFirstConsumer` binding always causes this
questions.explanation: Storage made its placement decision first, through `Immediate` binding or a pre-made PV, and now the pod has to follow the disk. `WaitForFirstConsumer` is the usual fix: it delays provisioning until the scheduler has picked a node.

questions.prompt: A pod has sat in Pending for 10 minutes and `describe` shows this. Why is silence the interesting part?
options: It's waiting on an image pull that hasn't started
The scheduler never picked it up — so check what's skipping it
Events expire quickly, so the silence means nothing
It's over quota, which doesn't produce events
questions.explanation: Silence is information. Check `.spec.schedulerName` and `.spec.schedulingGates` first. If every new pod in the cluster shows this, it's the scheduler component itself (file 03).

questions.prompt: STATUS shows `Init:1/2`. Where do you look?
options: The second init container's logs (`-c <name>`)
The previous container's logs (`--previous`)
The scheduler's logs in kube-system
The main container's logs (`kubectl logs checkout`)
questions.explanation: Init containers run strictly in order, and the main container doesn't exist until they all finish, so its logs are empty. 1/2 means one is done and the second is the blocker. A hang usually means it's waiting on a dependency that isn't up yet.

questions.prompt: A pod rescheduled after its old node died. Which layer is stuck?
questions.snippet:
STATUS: ContainerCreating
Warning  FailedAttachVolume  attachdetach-controller  Multi-Attach error for volume "pvc-abc123" Volume is already exclusively attached to one node and can't be attached to another
options: Scheduling — the scheduler picked the wrong zone
Storage — the RWO volume is still attached to the old node
Networking — the CNI can't assign an IP
The registry — the image is too large to pull
questions.explanation: Attach (to the node) and mount (into the pod) are separate steps. This one failed at attach because the old attachment wasn't released. `kubectl get volumeattachment` shows which node still holds it.

questions.prompt: The node is assigned and the image exists. What failed?
questions.snippet: Warning  FailedCreatePodSandBox  kubelet  Failed to create pod sandbox: plugin type="calico" failed: no IP addresses available in range
options: kube-proxy — Service rules weren't programmed
DNS — the pod can't resolve the registry
The app — it crashed before binding a port
CNI — the node's pod IP range is used up
questions.explanation: The sandbox (network namespace) is set up before any container runs. If the CNI can't hand out an IP, nothing else happens. This is a node-level networking problem, not an app problem, and it's often fixed by moving pods off a crowded node.

questions.prompt: Trap: you `kubectl apply` a Deployment and it succeeds, but no pods show up at all. The namespace has a ResourceQuota. Where's the error?
options: The pod's Events — quota errors show up there
The scheduler logs — quota is checked at placement
`kubectl describe rs` — the ReplicaSet's create was rejected
Nowhere — the pods are just slow to appear
questions.explanation: Quota is enforced when an object is created. With a bare pod, `apply` fails right away. With a Deployment, the Deployment object is accepted, and it's the ReplicaSet's later attempt to create pods that gets rejected. There are no pods to describe, so the error lives one level up.

questions.prompt: Trap: the pod isn't serving traffic. Is this a Pending-pod problem?
questions.snippet:
NAME       READY   STATUS             RESTARTS      AGE
checkout   0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   5 (40s ago)   4m
options: Pending — backoff means it's waiting to be placed
Pending — CrashLoopBackOff is an image problem
Not Pending — RESTARTS > 0 means it ran; it's a crash
Pending — READY 0/1 means it never started
questions.explanation: RESTARTS is the line between the two files: zero means nothing ever ran, nonzero means it ran and died. Walking an interviewer through scheduler checks for a crashing pod is the category mistake this flowchart exists to prevent.
